newsitem.title: UK: EMU sea change-traders must shape up or ship out.
newsitem.headline: EMU sea change-traders must shape up or ship out.

text.p: The expected introduction of a single European currency in January 1999 will mean a sea change on foreign exchanges, with dealers forced to shape up or ship out, seasoned market operators say.

But though the arrival of the "euro" will kill off dollar/mark -- the big fish of the forex world -- there is confidence that the market can both shift smoothly into its successor, dollar/euro, and find fresh sources of profit to replace the defunct mark crosses.

With dollar/mark -- which is estimated to account for around a fifth of global forex turnover -- currently hugging ever tighter ranges, some think the market will breathe a collective sigh of relief once the German currency bows out to the euro.

"The activity in dollar/mark is not exactly spectacular at the moment," said David Deakin, treasurer at Bank of Bermuda in Guernsey. "There will be a deal of relief if there's something to replace it."

But it may not all be plain sailing. Traders and investors will have to be flexible and innovative in their hunt for income sources to replace the mark crosses, which are trades against other European currencies.

The Australian and New Zealand dollars, the currencies of Eastern Europe and the so-called "tiger" economies of Asia, as well as units such as the Mexican peso, are all cited as potential plays for the mark-deprived investor.
"There are a lot more currencies to deal in than just the odd European one and I think people will concentrate on that," said a London-based treasury manager.
One veteran trader at a British merchant bank noted the already ongoing shift among banks out of trades such as dollar/French franc and dollar/Italian lira into dollar/mark and mark/franc.
"Obviously those will go out of the window, and the banks are diversifying even more and looking at some of the exotics to replace some of the ones coming out," he said.
Market mindsets will have to alter. Some foresee perceived trading blocs emerging, with dollar/euro thus reflecting the sale or purchase of the EU trading bloc against the U.S.
That suggests an enhanced role for euro/yen, mark/yen's replacement, as it is used to play Europe off against Asia.

"Whereas before you could diversify and buy a little bit of marks and a little bit of francs, you're going to have these massive shifts into one bloc," said the merchant bank trader. "It could cause more volatility in the long run."
Deakin at Bank of Bermuda believes the euro will be a true force to be reckoned with.

"I question whether people will think of the dollar as the be-all and end-all unit of account," he said. "They might, but there's no reason why they should when you've got something that has the clout of the European Union behind it."
While the amount of speculative trading will depend on the euro's stability against external currencies, trade flows should continue unabated, experienced market operators said.

"In terms of the trade part, there's no reason why the amount of euros needed to be bought and sold against the dollar should be any less than the sum of the currencies now bought and sold against the dollar," said Graham Cocks, vice-president, treasury at Bank of Boston in London.

Investment flows are tougher to predict. "That depends on the euro region's need for inward capital and its ability to export capital," said Cocks. The European drive to cut government debt should mean less bond issuance and that threatens to reduce investment streams, he added.
But as sovereign European currencies give way to the euro, just which economic data will operators use to make their trading decisions?
That question prompts many different answers.

Some reckon data from individual EU states will remain crucial as investors choose assets. The euro's arrival should minimise currency risk, leaving players to make decisions by weighing yield differential versus credit risk and assessing their ability to sell a bond on to someone else, they say.

Others believe national statistics, especially those of Germany and France, will be important in the early stages of monetary union but only until more countries join and pan-European data gathering really takes off.

Bank of Bermuda's Deakin said pan-Europe figures would be key. National data would be watched only "to the extent that people look at the Detroit purchasing managers' index or retail sales in the German states," he said. "U.S. trade figures are more interesting than Hawaii or Texas trade figures."
With confidence so high in the euro's credibility, the role of the Swiss franc might appear in jeopardy. But most are convinced it will always have a place in investors' hearts.

The franc should remain a safe haven from jitters over monetary union, and benefit as a potential EMU member if all goes well, market watchers said. It is also seen continuing to profit from faith in the Swiss economic and political system.

"The Swiss franc has the ability to win significantly if the whole thing (EMU) is messed up, yet even if it runs smoothly I don't see bundles of money coming screaming out of Switzerland into the euro," said Cocks at Bank of Boston.

One thing is sure. As European currencies are subsumed into the catch-all euro, forex traders must be adaptable if they are to survive in an unpredictable environment. For the inflexible mark cross trader the alternative is clear, said one treasury manager: "retirement".
"It's a question people joining the market or young people in the market will have," he said. "What will they be doing in three or five years time?"
